title: Both Can Be True: A Four-Minute Reflection for a Bittersweet Change
subtitle: A welcome beginning can carry a real sense of loss. This short, optional writing exercise makes room for both without demanding a verdict.
imageAlt: Two friends sit among moving boxes in a partly packed apartment, one holding a notebook while the other looks toward the open window.
imageConcept: A warm, natural-light scene of two friends sitting among half-packed boxes in a lived-in apartment. One writes in a small notebook; the other offers quiet company. Their expressions are thoughtful rather than staged or overtly sad, with familiar household details suggesting a meaningful move and a new beginning.
body: A change can be good news and still hurt

A move closer to family, a graduation, a new job, a child leaving home: changes that matter rarely arrive as a single clean feeling. You may be ready for what comes next and still miss the version of life that is ending. You might feel proud and unsettled, relieved and wistful. That combination is not proof that you chose wrongly, nor does it need to be tidied into gratitude before you are allowed to move forward.

Research on meaningful endings offers a useful frame. Across three studies involving graduation and memories of enjoyable experiences, researchers found that recalling good times could bring sadness alongside happiness, particularly when those experiences could not be repeated [1]. The finding does not mean every transition feels the same. It does suggest that tenderness about what is passing can coexist with pleasure about what is beginning. A small reflection can help name that complexity—not solve it.
Why the positive-spin reflex can miss something

People often reach for the reassuring line: “At least this is exciting,” or “You should be happy.” Sometimes that comfort lands. Sometimes it leaves the harder part unspoken. When a change is genuinely welcome, acknowledging what you will miss does not cancel your enthusiasm. It recognizes that a life can contain attachments worth grieving even as it opens into something worthwhile.

The reverse is true, too: allowing room for the difficult side does not require turning it into a warning. Mixed feelings are information about what matters to you, not an automatic instruction to stay, leave, celebrate or reconsider. This distinction matters because reflection can easily become a disguised test—an attempt to calculate whether you made the “right” choice. The practice here asks for no verdict. It simply gives two parts of the experience a place on the page.
What research can—and cannot—say about writing

There is some relevant research, but it is not a direct test of this exercise. In a randomized study, 40 undergraduate participants wrote about ambivalence concerning important goals across three sessions on consecutive days. The authors reported lower distress about ambivalence at follow-up among those in the expressive-writing group [2]. That is a small student sample and a longer, repeated exercise; it cannot establish that a four-minute reflection will produce the same result.

The wider expressive-writing literature is mixed. In a study of 833 adults recruited through a university research pool, participants completed 15-minute writing sessions over three days. Differences in outcomes appeared among participants who wrote longer essays, and the authors describe the findings as part of a literature with inconsistent results [3]. The proposed pause below is an editorial adaptation, not a validated intervention. Treat it as a way to notice and record what is present, not as a treatment or a promise of relief.
The four-minute “Both Can Be True” pause

Choose a change that feels manageable to consider—not the rawest or most painful part of your life. Use a scrap of paper or a private note. Set a four-minute timer if a boundary helps, or simply stop when you want. You do not need to write elegantly, explain the whole story or share the page with anyone.

Write one sentence beginning: “Something I’m glad about is…” Be specific if you can: having more time for a valued project, living nearer to someone, or seeing a loved one take a next step. Then write a second sentence: “Something I may miss, fear, or feel unsure about is…” It could be a familiar route, the ease of an old routine, or the uncertainty of being new somewhere. Complete the page with: “Both can be true; I don’t have to settle the whole question right now.”

That is the whole exercise. There is no required balance between the sentences, and you do not have to discover a lesson.

A useful reflection does not have to reach for a grand meaning. If you are moving, the thing you will miss may be the neighbor who watered your plants or the way afternoon light reaches the kitchen. If a child is leaving home, you can be glad for their independence and miss the ordinary noise of sharing a space. If you are starting a new role, pride in the opportunity can sit next to concern about losing colleagues or a familiar rhythm.

Keep the language close to what you actually know. “I’m excited to learn” and “I’m worried I won’t know anyone” can both be accurate without predicting how the transition will turn out. If you find yourself writing a case for or against the change, pause and return to description: what is welcome, and what feels tender or uncertain? The point is not to manufacture equal feelings. It is to stop one from having to erase the other.

Writing privately is enough. If you want another person involved, ask first whether they have space to listen, and say what would help: company, a few minutes without advice, or a practical conversation later. You can share only one sentence, paraphrase it, or keep the page to yourself. A supportive listener does not need to persuade you that everything will work out; they can acknowledge both sides without treating either as a problem to fix.

You can also stop before the four minutes are up. If a topic feels too raw, choose a smaller, more distant change or leave the exercise for another time. If writing makes you feel worse, close the page and do something grounding or contact someone you trust. This brief prompt is not professional care, and it is not a substitute for support when distress is persistent, overwhelming or interfering with daily life. Its modest purpose is simply to offer a little structure for a complicated moment.
A page for the day between boxes

If you want to try it, choose one specific transition already in front of you: the last week in an apartment, the first day after a graduation, or the evening before a new schedule begins. Put the page somewhere private and write only the two sentences. Then read them once as statements, not as evidence you must interpret. Close the notebook. Decide whether you want a small next step—asking someone to listen, taking a break from packing, or leaving the question alone until tomorrow. You do not have to feel resolved before the day continues. Let the welcome and the ache have their separate lines, and let the change remain unfinished for now.
